Article sectionDon’t Give the Inner Adult Away
Context immediately before

Say you grew up learning that what you wanted didn’t matter. Now you’re only just finding out what you actually think, maybe even learning to say no. Then somebody tells you there is no self. That might be freeing at another point in your life; right now it can sound a lot like the message you already know: what you want doesn’t matter. Or you tell a therapist, “No, that’s not right for me,” and they call it resistance. Maybe they’re right. But maybe they’re wrong about you, or taking you somewhere you don’t want to go. You still have to be able to say so.

Article sectionYour Body Might Need Some Love First
Context immediately before

Bring the challenge back gradually, and only when you want to and you’re recovering well. Some people try to toughen themselves up in a cauldron, but what you’re looking for is the edge where you can actually learn. And what about those hard dreams, or images that pop up during a session? They can show what feels important or frightening right now. Sometimes they show what feels missing, or what feels needed. They aren’t evidence that what you saw in them happened, though, and shouldn’t be used to confirm a memory or rebuild one. Or to suggest one.

Here’s where I want to clearly depart from the new-age wizdumb that all your problems are self-created: Somebody may really have crossed a boundary. That’s not just because they are your karmic partner mirroring what God wants to show you in yourself, even if that also applies sometimes. Your reaction is what you can control the most, though. If what they did hit something old in you, notice how that feels in your body. And notice how your feelings can also amplify or distort your perceptions of others. Just because your stomach tightened up doesn’t mean their boundary crossing indicates “They’re evil.” You can defer that judgement for when you’re in your happy place.

Feelings about yourself work the same way. “I feel attracted” or “I feel ashamed” is real as a feeling, but it doesn’t settle who you are, or who you love. Making too much out of something momentary is one side of the human psyche’s pendulum. Give yourself time to see what patterns form more durably, and what feels authentically yours vs something planted or manipulated into being there from society, influencers, family, friends, religion, etc., etc. You may find an exceptional freedom in exactly that in-between place where you don’t have to decide what your pronouns are, or whether you believe in this or that. If you stay in flux forever, though, it can seem like there’s nothing solid about you. In that case, sometimes it helps to meditate or talk with a good unbiased therapist who can help you see the pattern.

And reaching out doesn’t mean telling strangers everything. Privacy isn’t fakery. People can earn more of you by how they handle the smaller stuff, like whether that thing you told them about your weird fear of birds turns into a joke at the next party 🙈, and how they take it when you say no. But if a relationship is getting deep and you’re still keeping up a fake normal, happy version of yourself to hold onto it, I’d either bring more of the truth in, carefully, or let it be less deep for now. Then there’s the stuff that’s hardest to tell anyone, though it’s often exactly what you need help with. Maybe it’s an urge that scares you, or something you did that could get you in legal trouble. (An urge you’ve never acted on isn’t the same as something you did, by the way.) You know that DM you deleted? It can still be sitting on their phone as a screenshot 🙈, and whatever’s on a company’s server can get handed over if a court asks. A fake name doesn’t guarantee you’re anonymous, either. And some of the people you’d tell, like therapists, teachers, and doctors, can be required to report certain things (a few laws cover everybody, too). Which things depends on where you live, and it’s nowhere near every crime you might mention. The cops are hopefully the obvious ones to be careful with, even if they pretend to care.

Don’t be afraid to ask your therapist/yourself “What is this practice supposed to help, and how would I know if it’s helping?” This sovereign, gently curious stance should apply to everything in life. Feeling calmer or having deeper insights or explanations for the trauma response are some possible signs of initial progress, but if that’s the endgame, it’s just a cope. Real healing is ultimately measured by reduced need for the therapy. It’s like real parenting: you might start out reading parenting books and thinking hard about what to say or do, but after a while you get into the groove and a lot of it becomes natural. Inner parenting can be like that too. You don’t need to keep checking this guide or planning every conversation with your little one; the nurturing, protecting and guiding become more automatic. You might still turn to therapy when you need it, and life will keep offering chances to grow wiser and more compassionate. And if the therapy is actually working, it should improve your daily life, and especially the health of the inner child-inner adult relationship. Going at it harder isn’t as useful as going at it with more wisdom and compassion. Take the parts that work, and innovate on the rest.

Article sectionBorrow One Competency at a Time
Context immediately before

A complete ideal parent may be impossible to imagine (unless you saw The Brady Bunch). And imagination is pretty hard for adults anyway since it kinda gets stamped out of kids at an early age, but it’s not just a foolish waste of time. It’s actually a genius mode unlock. So since the adult is actually a baby when it comes to power to imagine, start small: Borrow one function at a time from a figure who embodies it. Perhaps a therapist or your grandmother really cared for you. Perhaps your teacher at some age was a great guide. Maybe an older sibling protected you well. And there’s always your future healed self if you can imagine that.

If you made a mistake, you can see how to repair that. You can renew your intention for tomorrow, getting better & better, every day, in every way. And enjoy your well-earned rest tonight.

Article sectionHear the Protective Part First
Context immediately before

That part doesn’t have to move out. It’s been living there way longer than the grown-up you. It can keep watch while you take one small step toward your little one, and I think watching is what it wants anyway, to find out if there’s a grown-up here now who could call it off if things got to be too much. Don’t be afraid to ask your therapist/yourself “What is this practice supposed to help, and how would I know if it’s helping?” This sovereign, gently curious stance should apply to everything in life. Feeling calmer or having deeper insights or explanations for the trauma response are some possible signs of initial progress, but if that’s the endgame, it’s just a cope. Real healing is ultimately measured by reduced need for the therapy. It’s like real parenting: you might start out reading parenting books and thinking hard about what to say or do, but after a while you get into the groove and a lot of it becomes natural. Inner parenting can be like that too. You don’t need to keep checking this guide or planning every conversation with your little one; the nurturing, protecting and guiding become more automatic. You might still turn to therapy when you need it, and life will keep offering chances to grow wiser and more compassionate. And if the therapy is actually working, it should improve your daily life, and especially the health of the inner child-inner adult relationship. Going at it harder isn’t as useful as going at it with more wisdom and compassion. Take the parts that work, and innovate on the rest.

So early on, the practice is finding out who’s actually in there, through long reflection with no outside input, and journaling just for yourself, without picturing a reader. You might catch yourself explaining who everybody is anyway. Focusing (Eugene Gendlin’s method of listening to a vague, felt sense in your body) can especially help you notice feelings and preferences the part you’ve been playing learned to overlook. Any words you put to them can stay tentative (”I hate cooking... or just for everybody?”) while you look at what they seem to mean and revise how you read them.

Part of building who you are is untangling yourself from whatever pulls you away from your own knowing in return for belonging. A political tribe might expect consistent positions and predictable reactions, while a family or religion that’s kind to you might have expectations that just feel like being good. Most groups expect some conformity, which is ordinary. Your family might want a particular kind of son or daughter, and your friends might have rules about what you can joke about or get upset about. But if going along means betraying yourself, that’s the bargain.

MovedInserted here — between the surrounding passages shown in context.
New insertion — there was no source passage at this position.
Inner-Child-r03-candidate.html · r0302

Then there’s another bargain, where you have to earn your worth: when you don’t feel your value inside as a human being, you can become a “human doer,” working for it in some arena outside yourself. That might be beauty, athleticism, sexual desirability, intelligence or grades. For some people it’s money or status, and for others it’s a sophisticated spiritual identity or becoming indispensable to everybody else’s problems. It can feel really good to be the one everybody calls. In the more shadowy presentation, when you really need to feel needed, you might be like the firefighters who become arsonists to keep themselves employed.

MovedInserted here — between the surrounding passages shown in context.
New insertion — there was no source passage at this position.

Even with good parents, you could have learned unhealthy self-valuation when people repeatedly praised what you did rather than your inherent worth. That wasn’t your flaw. Self-differentiation is learning to notice when you’re making that trade, and to keep your own ground instead.

    I think this is closer to Buddhist practice too. The point is not an impossible performance in which nothing unskillful ever appears. In one discourse (sutta), AN 6.63, the Buddha defines karma in terms of intention (so if you didn’t mean to cause harm, your mind is not poisoned). In DN 2, he explains that in the training to purify the mind, one first recognizes a fault, makes amends, and then restrains themself to prevent that kind of thing in future. So it’s not like, “you’re either pure, or you’re not,” which is where a lot of folks stay stuck. If you’re ashamed about something you chose to do, that might be a signal to give some attention to that. If it’s shame just because of an intrusive thought, then it’s probably not adaptive and can be simply let go of.

You know that DM you deleted? It can still be sitting on their phone as a screenshot 🙈, and whatever’s on a company’s server can get handed over if a court asks. A fake name doesn’t guarantee you’re anonymous, either. And some of the people you’d tell, like therapists, teachers, and doctors, can be required to report certain things (a few laws cover everybody, too). Which things depends on where you live, and it’s nowhere near every crime you might mention. The cops are hopefully the obvious ones to be careful with, even if they pretend to care.

Picture everything that had made them who they were by that moment, what happened to them and what they learned, the pain they carried and what they could and couldn’t handle. From in there, it was the only move they had. Hurt people often pass on pain they never worked through. You may have heard that from somebody telling you to forgive. When you see it for yourself, though, you might find yourself forgiving them, and if you’ve held them uniquely to blame, the rage can soften into something more accurate.

What’s left is fixing what can be fixed, and making it easier for something different to happen now. So a boundary can still be right. So can the law, if it comes to that, or telling them plainly it was wrong (or telling yourself, if they’d never hear it). Keeping away from them for good can be right too, and you can still forgive them from over there. Understanding somebody’s limitations should make my expectations more realistic, not make those limitations less consequential. “I understand how you became this way” can sit right next to “I now understand why I shouldn’t rely on you for this.”

    Before choosing a therapist, get to know the strengths and pitfalls of their approach, including any modifications they make to the standard protocol. I’d especially want to interview them regarding how they treat spiritual experiences. You want someone who won’t tell you what yours really mean, downplay them, force them, or treat them as a symptom. I’d also want one who doesn’t put ideas in your head, and who understands dissociation. What have they found too challenging to deal with so far, and where have they seen the best results? A good therapist won’t charge you an arm and a leg just for this kind of interview, and they should already have this information on their website to avoid wasting too much time. A certificate on the wall can’t tell you any of that.

    So early on, the practice is finding out who’s actually in there, through long reflection with no outside input, and journaling just for yourself, without picturing a reader. Time alone in nature helps too, and so does getting back the preferences that got buried: the foods you really like and what feels good to do, and what you believe and feel when nobody’s around to take your cues from. Any words you put to them can stay tentative (”I hate cooking... or just for everybody?”) while you look at what they seem to mean and revise how you read them.

    Part of building who you are is untangling yourself from whatever pulls you away from your own knowing in return for belonging. A political tribe might expect consistent positions and predictable reactions, while a family or religion that’s kind to you might have expectations that just feel like being good. Most groups expect some conformity, which is ordinary. Your family might want a particular kind of son or daughter, and your friends might have rules about what you can joke about or get upset about. But if going along means betraying yourself, that’s the bargain.

    Then there’s another bargain, where you have to earn your worth: when you don’t feel your value inside as a human being, you can become a “human doer,” working for it in some arena outside yourself. That might be beauty, athleticism, sexual desirability, intelligence or grades. For some people it’s money or status, and for others it’s a sophisticated spiritual identity or becoming indispensable to everybody else’s problems. It can feel really good to be the one everybody calls. In the more shadowy presentation, when you really need to feel needed, you might be like the firefighters who become arsonists to keep themselves employed.

You might still be enjoying one of those when your little one starts asking how long this is going to last.

    I think this is closer to Buddhist practice too. The point is not an impossible performance in which nothing unskillful ever appears. In one discourse (sutta), AN 6.63, the Buddha defines karma in terms of intention (so if you didn’t mean to cause harm, your mind is not poisoned). In DN 2, he explains that in the training to purify the mind, one first recognizes a fault, makes amends, and then restrains themself to prevent that kind of thing in future. So it’s not like, “you’re either pure, or you’re not,” which is where a lot of folks stay stuck. If you’re ashamed about something you chose to do, that might be a signal to give some attention to that. If it’s shame just because of an intrusive thought, then it’s probably not adaptive and can be simply let go of.

Picture everything that had made them who they were by that moment, what happened to them and what they learned, the pain they carried and what they could and couldn’t handle. From in there, it was the only move they had. Hurt people often pass on pain they never worked through. You may have heard that from somebody telling you to forgive. What’s left is fixing what can be fixed, and making it easier for something different to happen now. So a boundary can still be right. So can the law, if it comes to that, or telling them plainly it was wrong (or telling yourself, if they’d never hear it). Keeping away from them for good can be right too, and you can still forgive them from over there. Understanding somebody’s limitations should make my expectations more realistic, not make those limitations less consequential. “I understand how you became this way” can sit right next to “I now understand why I shouldn’t rely on you for this.”

    Your little one can get really loud in the gap after one life ends and before the next one has formed. Tibetan Buddhism calls an in-between state a bardo . You don’t have to buy what it teaches about death and rebirth to use the everyday part: endings leave a stretch where the old you is gone and the new one hasn’t shown up.

That’s easy to lose sight of when you’ve spent so long looking at them. And you aren’t alone. There’s help, and lots of other people are out there learning to look after their own little ones.

    The best licensed, listed therapists you’ll find that come close will be doing Internal Family Systems (IFS), or Schema Therapy. I’ll talk more about those next, but Schema Therapy comes closest to my approach. Open Path Collective (or a similar resource in your country) lists thousands of affordable therapists. You can filter them by Schema or IFS. You can often find even more Schema therapists at the official site .

    Before choosing a therapist, get to know the strengths and pitfalls of their approach, including any modifications they make to the standard protocol. I’d especially want to interview them regarding how they treat spiritual experiences. You want someone who won’t tell you what yours really mean, downplay them, force them, or treat them as a symptom. I’d also want one who doesn’t put ideas in your head, and who understands dissociation. What have they found too challenging to deal with so far, and where have they seen the best results? A good therapist won’t charge you an arm and a leg just for this kind of interview, and they should already have this information on their website to avoid wasting too much time. A certificate on the wall can’t tell you any of that.

That doesn’t mean you can’t get a lot of great insights sometimes when talking to AI, though, but just expect it to go sideways sometimes.
